meta.subject: Physics
meta.rendering_note: Every progressive wave follows the locked \( y=A\sin(kx-\omega t+\phi) \) convention for travel along +x (a plus sign between kx and the time term means travel along -x). Every Greek-letter symbol (omega, lambda, mu, gamma, phi) is written as a single KaTeX span, no raw Unicode math symbols appear anywhere, explanations separate steps with double line breaks, and every numeric correct answer terminates cleanly.

topics.name: Transverse and Longitudinal Waves: the Wave Equation and Speed of a Wave
topics.summary: A mechanical wave is a travelling disturbance that carries energy through a medium without carrying the medium along. In a transverse wave the particles vibrate perpendicular to the direction of travel (waves on a string); in a longitudinal wave they vibrate along it (sound in air). A sinusoidal wave moving along the positive x-direction is written \( y=A\sin(kx-\omega t+\phi) \), where A is the amplitude, \( k=2\pi/\lambda \) is the angular wave number, \( \omega=2\pi f \) is the angular frequency and \( \phi \) is the phase constant. The minus sign goes with travel along +x; a plus sign means travel along -x. The wave speed is \( v=\omega/k=f\lambda \). Each particle performs SHM, so its velocity is at most \( A\omega \) and its acceleration is \( -\omega^2y \), both quite different from the wave speed. On a stretched string the speed is fixed by the string and its tension, \( v=\sqrt{T/\mu} \), where \( \mu \) is mass per unit length; changing the source frequency changes only the wavelength.
topics.worked_example: For \( y=0.05\sin(2x-10t) \) (SI): \( k=2 \), \( \omega=10 \), so \( v=\omega/k=5 \) m/s along +x, and the maximum particle speed is \( A\omega=0.5 \) m/s.
common_mistakes: Treating \( kx+\omega t \) as travel along +x; in this form the minus sign means +x
Using \( v=\omega k \) or \( v=f/\lambda \) instead of \( v=\omega/k=f\lambda \)
Thinking wave speed on a string changes with frequency or amplitude
Using total mass instead of mass per unit length in \( \sqrt{T/\mu} \)
Confusing particle speed \( A\omega \) with wave speed \( \omega/k \)

topics.name: Speed of Sound and Waves in Different Media
topics.summary: Sound is a longitudinal mechanical wave, so it needs a medium and cannot cross a vacuum. Its speed depends on the elasticity and density of the medium: \( v=\sqrt{Y/\rho} \) in a solid rod, \( v=\sqrt{B/\rho} \) in a liquid, and \( v=\sqrt{\gamma P/\rho} \) in a gas. Newton assumed isothermal compressions and wrote \( \sqrt{P/\rho} \), which came out about 15 percent too low; Laplace pointed out that the compressions are adiabatic, so the bulk modulus is \( \gamma P \). Since \( P/\rho=RT/M \), the speed in a gas is \( \sqrt{\gamma RT/M} \): it rises as \( \sqrt T \) (T in kelvin), falls with molar mass, and does not change with pressure at fixed temperature. Moist air, being lighter, carries sound slightly faster. Sound is generally fastest in solids, slower in liquids and slowest in gases. When sound passes from one medium to another, the frequency stays fixed by the source while speed and wavelength both change.
key_formulas: \( v\propto\sqrt T \) for a given gas
topics.worked_example: Air at 300 K carries sound at 340 m/s. At 1200 K: \( v=340\times\sqrt{1200/300}=680 \) m/s.
common_mistakes: Using Newton's \( \sqrt{P/\rho} \) and dropping \( \gamma \)
Taking \( v\propto T \) instead of \( \sqrt T \)
Forgetting to convert Celsius to kelvin
Thinking higher pressure alone raises sound speed at constant temperature
Thinking frequency changes when sound enters a new medium

topics.name: Superposition, Reflection, and Standing Waves
topics.summary: When waves overlap, the net displacement is the algebraic sum of the individual displacements (superposition), and each wave continues unchanged afterwards. Two coherent in-phase sources interfere constructively where the path difference is \( n\lambda \) and destructively where it is \( (n+\tfrac12)\lambda \). For two equal waves with phase difference \( \phi \), the resultant amplitude is \( 2A\cos(\phi/2) \). At a rigid boundary a wave reflects with a phase change of \( \pi \) (inverted); at a free end it reflects with no phase change. Two identical waves travelling in opposite directions, \( A\sin(kx-\omega t) \) and \( A\sin(kx+\omega t) \), add to a standing wave \( y=2A\sin kx\cos\omega t \). Its nodes (zero amplitude) are \( \lambda/2 \) apart, antinodes (amplitude \( 2A \)) lie midway, and node-to-antinode is \( \lambda/4 \). All particles within one loop move in phase; neighbouring loops move in opposite phase. A standing wave carries no net energy along the medium.
key_formulas: Nodes at \( x=n\lambda/2 \); antinodes at \( x=(n+\tfrac12)\lambda/2 \)
topics.worked_example: For \( y=0.04\sin(5\pi x)\cos(100\pi t) \): \( \lambda=2\pi/5\pi=0.4 \) m, so nodes are 0.2 m apart and each component wave has amplitude 0.02 m.
common_mistakes: Mixing up node-to-node (\( \lambda/2 \)) with node-to-antinode (\( \lambda/4 \))
Forgetting the inversion on reflection from a rigid end
Taking the standing-wave amplitude \( 2A \) as the component amplitude
Thinking a standing wave has no component waves moving at all
Using \( (n+\tfrac12)\lambda \) for constructive interference

topics.name: Normal Modes of Stretched Strings and Organ Pipes
topics.summary: A standing wave can only fit into a bounded system in certain patterns, called normal modes. A string fixed at both ends has a node at each end, so \( L=n\lambda/2 \) and \( f_n=nv/2L \) for n = 1, 2, 3, ...; all harmonics are present. A pipe open at both ends has a displacement antinode at each end and also gives \( f_n=nv/2L \) with all harmonics. A pipe closed at one end has a displacement node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end, so only odd numbers of quarter wavelengths fit: \( f=(2n-1)v/4L \). Its fundamental \( v/4L \) is half that of an open pipe of the same length, and it has only odd harmonics, so its first overtone is the third harmonic. Overtones are counted from the first frequency higher than the fundamental. For a sonometer, \( f_1=\frac{1}{2L}\sqrt{T/\mu} \). When an end correction e is given, it adds to the length at each open end.
key_formulas: Closed pipe with end correction: \( f_1=v/4(L+e) \)
Open pipe with end correction: \( f_1=v/2(L+2e) \)
topics.worked_example: A pipe 0.85 m long closed at one end, with \( v=340 \) m/s, has \( f_1=340/3.4=100 \) Hz; its next resonances are 300 Hz and 500 Hz, never 200 Hz or 400 Hz.
common_mistakes: Using \( v/2L \) for a closed pipe
Allowing even harmonics in a closed pipe
Swapping node and antinode at closed or open ends
Calling the second harmonic the second overtone
Ignoring a stated end correction, or adding it only once for an open pipe

topics.name: Beats and the Doppler Effect
topics.summary: When two sounds of slightly different frequencies \( f_1 \) and \( f_2 \) superpose, the loudness rises and falls periodically; the number of beats per second is \( |f_1-f_2| \), and the pitch heard is close to the average frequency. Loading a tuning fork with wax lowers its frequency, while filing a prong raises it; watching whether beats increase or decrease identifies an unknown frequency. The Doppler effect is the change in heard frequency caused by motion of the source or observer along the line joining them. With v the speed of sound, \( f'=f\dfrac{v\pm v_o}{v\mp v_s} \), using the upper signs when source and observer move towards each other and the lower signs when they move apart. Approach always raises the heard frequency; recession always lowers it. A moving source changes the wavelength in the medium, while a moving observer only changes how often crests are met. An echo from a wall involves two shifts: the wall first acts as an observer, then as a source.
key_formulas: General: \( f'=f\,\dfrac{v\pm v_o}{v\mp v_s} \) (upper signs for approach)
Wavelength ahead of a moving source: \( (v-v_s)/f \)
topics.worked_example: A 450 Hz source approaches at 34 m/s with \( v=340 \) m/s: \( f'=450\times340/306=500 \) Hz. Receding at the same speed, a 550 Hz source is heard at \( 550\times340/374=500 \) Hz.
common_mistakes: Taking the sum or average of frequencies as the beat frequency
Flipping Doppler signs so frequency falls on approach
Using the moving-observer formula for a moving source, or vice versa
Forgetting that wax lowers and filing raises a fork's frequency
Applying only one Doppler shift for an echo from a wall

questions.topic: Transverse and Longitudinal Waves: the Wave Equation and Speed of a Wave
questions.question: In a transverse wave travelling along a stretched string, the particles of the string vibrate in which direction?
options: Perpendicular to the direction in which the wave travels
Parallel to the direction in which the wave travels
Forward along with the wave, carrying the string material to the far end
In small circles in the plane containing the string
questions.explanation:
In a transverse wave the displacement of each particle is perpendicular to the direction of propagation.

On a string the wave moves along the string while each element moves sideways, up and down, about its mean position.
questions.hint: Transverse means 'across'. Think about a rope flicked up and down.
distractor_logic: This describes a longitudinal wave, not a transverse one
Confuses transport of energy with transport of matter; particles only oscillate about their mean positions
Borrows the motion of surface water particles, which is not how a stretched string vibrates

questions.topic: Transverse and Longitudinal Waves: the Wave Equation and Speed of a Wave
questions.question: A sound wave travelling through air is an example of which type of wave?
options: A wave that needs no medium at all
Transverse in air but longitudinal in water
questions.explanation:
Sound travels as a series of compressions and rarefactions.

The air particles oscillate back and forth along the direction in which the sound travels, so the wave is longitudinal. Being carried by the particles of air, it is a mechanical wave.
questions.hint: Picture a slinky pushed and pulled along its length.
distractor_logic: Air cannot sustain the shear needed for transverse waves; its particles oscillate along the direction of travel
Sound is a mechanical wave and needs a material medium to travel
Reverses nothing useful: fluids support only longitudinal mechanical waves, in air as well as in water

questions.topic: Transverse and Longitudinal Waves: the Wave Equation and Speed of a Wave
questions.question: Which relation correctly connects wave speed \( v \), frequency \( f \) and wavelength \( \lambda \)?
questions.explanation:
In one period \( T \) the wave advances by exactly one wavelength.

So \( v=\lambda/T \), and since \( f=1/T \), \( v=f\lambda \).
questions.hint: In one time period, how far does the wave move forward?
distractor_logic: Divides instead of multiplies, the speed-formula version of Trap A
Inverts the role of frequency; this has units of metre-seconds, not metres per second
Adds two quantities with different units, which is dimensionally meaningless

questions.topic: Transverse and Longitudinal Waves: the Wave Equation and Speed of a Wave
questions.question: A wave has frequency 50 Hz and wavelength 4 m. What is its speed?
questions.explanation:
Use \( v=f\lambda \).

\( v=50\times4=200 \) m/s.
questions.hint: Speed equals frequency times wavelength.
distractor_logic: Uses \( v=f/\lambda \) instead of \( v=f\lambda \)
Uses \( v=\lambda/f \), which inverts the frequency
Adds frequency and wavelength instead of multiplying them

questions.topic: Transverse and Longitudinal Waves: the Wave Equation and Speed of a Wave
questions.question: A wave is described by \( y=A\sin(kx-\omega t) \) with \( k \) and \( \omega \) positive. In which direction does it travel?
options: It does not travel; it is a standing wave
questions.explanation:
Keep the phase \( kx-\omega t \) constant to follow one crest.

As \( t \) increases, \( x \) must also increase to keep \( kx-\omega t \) fixed, so the crest moves towards positive x.

The minus sign between \( kx \) and \( \omega t \) goes with travel along +x.
questions.hint: Follow a crest: if t grows, what must x do to keep the phase the same?
distractor_logic: Trap A: associates the minus sign with negative-direction travel, the reverse of the correct rule
Mixes up the direction of particle displacement (y) with the direction of wave travel (x)
A single sine of \( kx-\omega t \) is a travelling wave; a standing wave needs a product like \( \sin kx\cos\omega t \)

questions.topic: Transverse and Longitudinal Waves: the Wave Equation and Speed of a Wave
questions.question: How is the angular wave number \( k \) related to the wavelength \( \lambda \)?
questions.explanation:
Over one wavelength the phase \( kx \) must change by \( 2\pi \).

So \( k\lambda=2\pi \), which gives \( k=2\pi/\lambda \).
questions.hint: One full wavelength corresponds to one full cycle of phase.
distractor_logic: Inverts the relation; a longer wavelength should give a smaller k
Multiplies instead of divides, so k would grow with wavelength
Drops the \( 2\pi \) factor that converts cycles into radians

questions.topic: Transverse and Longitudinal Waves: the Wave Equation and Speed of a Wave
questions.question: The speed of a transverse wave on a stretched string with tension \( T \) and linear mass density \( \mu \) is:
options: \( v=\sqrt{T/M} \), where \( M \) is the total mass of the string
questions.explanation:
A tighter string pulls a displaced element back faster, so speed rises with \( T \).

A heavier string per metre responds more slowly, so speed falls with \( \mu \).

Together, \( v=\sqrt{T/\mu} \), where \( \mu \) is mass per unit length.
questions.hint: Tension helps the wave, inertia per metre slows it down.
distractor_logic: Trap B: swaps tension and linear mass density, so a heavier string would carry waves faster
Leaves out the square root, which also gives wrong units
Trap B: uses total mass instead of mass per unit length

questions.topic: Transverse and Longitudinal Waves: the Wave Equation and Speed of a Wave
questions.question: A wave pulse travels along a long rope from one end to the other. What does the wave carry along the rope?
options: The rope's material itself, moving from one end to the other
Both the rope's material and energy
Only the shape of the pulse, with no energy at all
Energy, without carrying the rope's material along
questions.explanation:
Each piece of the rope moves and then returns to its mean position.

What travels is the disturbance, and with it energy and momentum, not the rope itself.
questions.hint: After the pulse passes, where is each bit of rope?
distractor_logic: Confuses the motion of the disturbance with the motion of the medium
Particles only oscillate about fixed mean positions, so no net material is transported
A wave does transfer energy; it is exactly what makes the far end move

questions.topic: Speed of Sound and Waves in Different Media
questions.question: Through which of the following can sound NOT travel?
questions.explanation:
Sound is a mechanical wave: it needs particles of a medium to pass on compressions and rarefactions.

A vacuum has no particles, so sound cannot travel through it.
questions.hint: Sound needs something to push against.
distractor_logic: Liquids carry sound well as longitudinal waves
Solids carry sound, in fact faster than gases do
Any gas can carry sound; a light gas like hydrogen carries it quite fast

questions.topic: Speed of Sound and Waves in Different Media
questions.question: In which of these media is the speed of sound usually the greatest?
questions.explanation:
Speed of sound depends on the elasticity of the medium divided by its density.

Solids like steel have very large elastic moduli, so sound is fastest in them, then liquids, then gases.
questions.hint: Stiffer media pass on disturbances faster.
distractor_logic: Gases are the least stiff and give the lowest speeds
Water is faster than air but far less stiff than steel
Sound cannot travel in a vacuum at all

questions.topic: Speed of Sound and Waves in Different Media
questions.question: Laplace corrected Newton's formula for the speed of sound in a gas by replacing the pressure \( P \) with:
questions.explanation:
Newton assumed isothermal compressions, giving \( v=\sqrt{P/\rho} \), which came out too low.

Laplace treated them as adiabatic, where the bulk modulus is \( \gamma P \).

So \( v=\sqrt{\gamma P/\rho} \).
questions.hint: Adiabatic bulk modulus of a gas.
distractor_logic: Divides by \( \gamma \), which would make the corrected speed smaller than Newton's value
Squares the ratio of specific heats, overcorrecting
Uses an arbitrary factor unrelated to the adiabatic nature of sound

questions.topic: Speed of Sound and Waves in Different Media
questions.question: Laplace assumed that the compressions and rarefactions of a sound wave in air take place:
questions.explanation:
The oscillations are so fast that there is no time for heat to flow in or out of a compressed layer.

So the process is adiabatic, and the bulk modulus becomes \( \gamma P \).
questions.hint: Think about how quickly the air is squeezed and released.
distractor_logic: This was Newton's assumption, which gave a speed about 15 percent too low
Pressure is exactly what varies in a sound wave
The volume of each layer of air changes as it is compressed and expanded

questions.topic: Speed of Sound and Waves in Different Media
questions.question: The speed of a longitudinal wave in a solid rod of Young's modulus \( Y \) and density \( \rho \) is:
questions.explanation:
For any medium, \( v=\sqrt{\text{elastic modulus}/\text{density}} \).

For a thin solid rod the relevant modulus is Young's modulus, giving \( v=\sqrt{Y/\rho} \).
questions.hint: Elasticity over inertia, under a square root.
distractor_logic: Inverts the ratio, so denser rods would carry sound faster
Leaves out the square root; the units are then \( \mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}} \)
Applies the gas-only Laplace factor \( \gamma \) to a solid

questions.topic: Speed of Sound and Waves in Different Media
questions.question: A sound wave passes from air into water. Which of its properties stays the same?
questions.explanation:
Frequency is set by the source; each crest arriving at the boundary produces one crest on the other side.

Speed changes with the medium, so from \( v=f\lambda \) the wavelength changes too.
questions.hint: What does the source control?
distractor_logic: Wavelength changes because speed changes while frequency is fixed
Speed is set by the medium and is much larger in water
Both change; only frequency, set by the source, is unchanged

questions.topic: Speed of Sound and Waves in Different Media
questions.question: The pressure of a gas is doubled while its temperature is kept constant. What happens to the speed of sound in it?
options: It increases by a factor of \( \sqrt2 \)
questions.explanation:
At constant temperature, \( P/\rho \) stays constant (it equals \( RT/M \)).

So \( v=\sqrt{\gamma P/\rho} \) is unchanged.
questions.hint: What happens to density when pressure doubles at fixed temperature?
distractor_logic: Looks only at P in \( \sqrt{\gamma P/\rho} \) and forgets that density doubles as well
Assumes the extra density alone matters and ignores the rise in pressure
Treats speed as directly proportional to pressure

questions.topic: Speed of Sound and Waves in Different Media
questions.question: The absolute temperature of air is made four times. The speed of sound in it becomes:
questions.explanation:
\( v=\sqrt{\gamma RT/M} \), so \( v\propto\sqrt T \).

Four times T gives \( \sqrt4=2 \) times v.
questions.hint: Speed of sound goes as the square root of absolute temperature.
distractor_logic: Takes speed proportional to T instead of to \( \sqrt T \)
Trap B confusion: temperature is a property of the medium and does change the speed
Reverses the dependence, as if hotter air slowed sound

questions.topic: Superposition, Reflection, and Standing Waves
questions.question: According to the principle of superposition, when two waves overlap, the resultant displacement at a point is:
options: The algebraic sum of the displacements due to each wave
The product of the two individual displacements
Equal to the larger of the two displacements
The average of the two displacements
questions.explanation:
Each wave produces its own displacement independently.

Where they overlap, the net displacement is \( y=y_1+y_2 \), with signs taken into account.
questions.hint: Displacements with signs simply add.
distractor_logic: Multiplication has no physical basis here; displacements add
Ignores the contribution of the smaller wave
Divides by two, which would halve the combined effect

questions.topic: Superposition, Reflection, and Standing Waves
questions.question: In a standing wave, what is the distance between two consecutive nodes?
questions.explanation:
Nodes of \( y=2A\sin kx\cos\omega t \) occur where \( \sin kx=0 \), i.e. \( kx=n\pi \).

So \( x=n\lambda/2 \): consecutive nodes are \( \lambda/2 \) apart.
questions.hint: Where does \( \sin kx \) vanish?
distractor_logic: Gives the distance between alternate nodes
Gives the node-to-antinode distance
Doubles a full wavelength; nodes are much closer than that

questions.topic: Superposition, Reflection, and Standing Waves
questions.question: In a standing wave, what is the distance between a node and the nearest antinode?
questions.explanation:
Nodes are \( \lambda/2 \) apart and antinodes lie midway between them.

So a node and its nearest antinode are \( \lambda/4 \) apart.
questions.hint: Antinodes sit halfway between nodes.
distractor_logic: Gives the node-to-node distance
Gives a full wavelength
Halves the correct value once too often

questions.topic: Superposition, Reflection, and Standing Waves
questions.question: When a wave on a string reflects from a rigidly fixed end, the reflected wave undergoes a phase change of:
questions.explanation:
At a rigid end the displacement must always be zero.

This forces the reflected wave to be inverted, which is a phase change of \( \pi \).
questions.hint: The fixed end cannot move; how must the reflected wave cancel the incident one there?
distractor_logic: This happens at a free end, not a rigid end
A quarter-cycle shift does not satisfy zero displacement at the fixed end
An arbitrary fraction with no link to the boundary condition

questions.topic: Superposition, Reflection, and Standing Waves
questions.question: An upward pulse on a string reaches an end that is free to move up and down. The reflected pulse is:
options: Absent, because a free end absorbs the pulse fully
Upward but moving in the same direction as before
questions.explanation:
At a free end there is no restoring pull from beyond the end, so the end overshoots.

The pulse reflects with no phase change: it returns upright.
questions.hint: Free end: no phase change.
distractor_logic: This is what happens at a rigid end
A free end reflects the pulse; it does not absorb it
A reflected pulse must travel back the way it came

questions.topic: Superposition, Reflection, and Standing Waves
questions.question: Two coherent sources emit waves in phase. At a point, the waves interfere constructively when the path difference is:
options: \( n\lambda \), where n is an integer
questions.explanation:
Constructive interference needs crests to meet crests.

This happens when one path is longer by a whole number of wavelengths: \( \Delta=n\lambda \).
questions.hint: Crest meets crest when the extra path is a whole number of wavelengths.
distractor_logic: This is the condition for destructive interference
Quarter-wavelength steps include points of partial and destructive interference
Has units of inverse length, so it cannot be a path difference

questions.topic: Superposition, Reflection, and Standing Waves
questions.question: At a node of a standing wave on a string, the particle of the string:
options: Vibrates with amplitude equal to twice that of each component wave
Stays at rest at all times
Passes energy along the string at the wave speed
questions.explanation:
A node is a point where the two component waves always cancel.

So its displacement is zero at every instant.
questions.hint: Node means 'no motion'.
distractor_logic: Describes an antinode, not a node
That amplitude, \( 2A \), occurs at antinodes
A standing wave does not transport energy past its nodes

questions.topic: Superposition, Reflection, and Standing Waves
questions.question: Which statement about a standing wave on a string is correct?
options: It transports energy along the string at the wave speed
Its pattern moves along the string at twice the wave speed
All points on the string vibrate with the same amplitude
It does not transport energy along the string
questions.explanation:
A standing wave is the sum of two equal waves travelling in opposite directions.

Their energy flows cancel, so no net energy moves past a node; energy only sloshes between adjacent nodes.
questions.hint: What does 'standing' mean for the pattern?
distractor_logic: That is a property of a single travelling wave
The pattern stays in place; that is why it is called standing
Amplitude varies from zero at nodes to maximum at antinodes

questions.topic: Normal Modes of Stretched Strings and Organ Pipes
questions.question: The fundamental frequency of a string of length L fixed at both ends, with wave speed v, is:
questions.explanation:
With a node at each end, the simplest pattern has one loop: \( L=\lambda/2 \).

So \( \lambda=2L \) and \( f_1=v/2L \).
questions.hint: One loop fits between the fixed ends.
distractor_logic: Trap C: uses the closed-pipe fundamental for a string
Takes the whole length as one wavelength, which is the second harmonic
Inverts the half-wavelength relation

questions.topic: Normal Modes of Stretched Strings and Organ Pipes
questions.question: The fundamental frequency of a pipe of length L closed at one end, with sound speed v, is:
questions.explanation:
A closed end is a displacement node and an open end is an antinode.

The simplest fit is a quarter wavelength: \( L=\lambda/4 \).

So \( f_1=v/4L \).
questions.hint: Node to antinode is a quarter wavelength.
distractor_logic: Trap C: uses the open-pipe or string fundamental
Treats the pipe length as a full wavelength
Inverts the quarter-wavelength relation

questions.topic: Normal Modes of Stretched Strings and Organ Pipes
questions.question: Which harmonics are present in a pipe closed at one end?
questions.explanation:
The pipe must fit an odd number of quarter wavelengths: \( L=(2n-1)\lambda/4 \).

So \( f=(2n-1)v/4L \): only 1, 3, 5, ... times the fundamental.
questions.hint: Node at one end, antinode at the other: count quarter wavelengths.
distractor_logic: Trap C: true for strings and open pipes, not for closed pipes
Reverses the rule, and would even exclude the fundamental
Closed pipes do support overtones, namely the odd harmonics

questions.topic: Normal Modes of Stretched Strings and Organ Pipes
questions.question: For sound in a pipe, what is found at the closed end?
options: Both a displacement node and a displacement antinode
Neither, since the closed end has no effect on the pattern
questions.explanation:
Air at a closed end cannot move into the wall.

So its displacement is always zero: a displacement node.
questions.hint: Can the air move through a solid wall?
distractor_logic: Trap C: swaps the closed-end condition with the open-end one
A point cannot be both at once
The closed end fixes the boundary condition

questions.topic: Normal Modes of Stretched Strings and Organ Pipes
questions.question: For a pipe open at both ends, what are the conditions at the two ends?
options: A displacement antinode at each end
A displacement node at each end
A node at one end and an antinode at the other
Nodes or antinodes depending on the frequency
questions.explanation:
At an open end the air is free to move in and out.

So both ends are displacement antinodes, and the fundamental has \( L=\lambda/2 \).
questions.hint: Air is free to move at an open end.
distractor_logic: Trap C: that is the condition for a string fixed at both ends
Trap C: that is the closed-pipe condition
The end conditions are fixed by the open ends, not by frequency

questions.topic: Normal Modes of Stretched Strings and Organ Pipes
questions.question: A string 0.5 m long, fixed at both ends, carries waves at 100 m/s. What is its fundamental frequency?
questions.hint: Use \( v/2L \).
distractor_logic: Trap C: uses \( v/4L \), the closed-pipe formula
Uses \( v/L \), taking the string length as a full wavelength
Uses \( v/8L \), halving the closed-pipe value again

questions.topic: Normal Modes of Stretched Strings and Organ Pipes
questions.question: An open pipe 0.85 m long is in air where sound travels at 340 m/s. What is its fundamental frequency?
questions.hint: Antinodes at both ends, like one loop.
distractor_logic: Trap C: uses the closed-pipe formula \( v/4L \)
Uses \( v/L \), which gives the second harmonic
Multiplies speed by length instead of dividing

questions.topic: Normal Modes of Stretched Strings and Organ Pipes
questions.question: For a pipe closed at one end, the second overtone is which harmonic?
questions.explanation:
A closed pipe has only odd harmonics: 1st, 3rd, 5th, ...

Overtones are the frequencies higher than the fundamental: first overtone = 3rd harmonic, second overtone = 5th harmonic.
questions.hint: List the allowed harmonics, then count overtones after the fundamental.
distractor_logic: That is the first overtone
Trap C: assumes even harmonics exist in a closed pipe
Trap C: counts even harmonics as overtones

questions.topic: Beats and the Doppler Effect
questions.question: Two tuning forks of frequencies 256 Hz and 260 Hz are sounded together. How many beats are heard per second?
questions.explanation:
Beat frequency \( =|f_1-f_2| \).

\( |256-260|=4 \) beats per second.
questions.hint: Beats count the difference, not the sum.
distractor_logic: Trap D: adds the frequencies instead of taking their difference
Trap D: gives the average frequency, which is the pitch heard, not the beat rate
Halves the difference

questions.topic: Beats and the Doppler Effect
questions.question: Beats are produced when:
options: Two waves of equal frequency travel in opposite directions
Two sound waves of slightly different frequencies superpose
A sound wave reflects from a hard wall
A source moves towards a listener
questions.explanation:
Two nearby frequencies drift in and out of step.

When in step the sound is loud, when out of step it is soft; this periodic rise and fall is beats.
questions.hint: Think of two notes that are almost, but not quite, the same.
distractor_logic: That produces a standing wave
Reflection alone gives an echo, not beats
That is the Doppler effect, a change in heard frequency

questions.topic: Beats and the Doppler Effect
questions.question: A source of sound of frequency f moves towards a stationary observer with speed \( v_s \). If v is the speed of sound, the frequency heard is:
questions.explanation:
An approaching source crowds the wavefronts in front of it, shortening the wavelength to \( (v-v_s)/f \).

The observer hears \( f'=v/\lambda'=f\,v/(v-v_s) \), which is higher than f.
questions.hint: Approaching source: frequency must go up; the source speed belongs in the denominator.
distractor_logic: Trap D: this is the receding-source formula, giving a lower frequency on approach
Trap D: puts the source speed in the numerator, like an observer, with the wrong sign
Treats the source as if it were a moving observer

questions.topic: Beats and the Doppler Effect
questions.question: An observer moves with speed \( v_o \) towards a stationary source of frequency f. If v is the speed of sound, the frequency heard is:
questions.explanation:
The wavelength in air is unchanged since the source is at rest.

Moving towards the source, the observer meets waves at relative speed \( v+v_o \).

\( f'=(v+v_o)/\lambda=f\,(v+v_o)/v \).
questions.hint: Approaching observer: meets crests more often.
distractor_logic: Trap D: this is for an observer moving away, giving a lower frequency on approach
Uses the moving-source form for a moving observer
Trap D: puts the observer speed in the denominator with a sign that lowers the frequency

questions.topic: Beats and the Doppler Effect
questions.question: Wax is stuck on one prong of a tuning fork. Its frequency:
questions.explanation:
Adding mass to the prong increases its inertia.

A heavier prong vibrates more slowly, so the frequency falls. (Filing a prong does the opposite.)
questions.hint: More mass, slower vibration.
distractor_logic: Reverses the effect; extra mass slows the vibration
Ignores the added mass
A little wax only lowers the frequency; the fork still vibrates

questions.topic: Beats and the Doppler Effect
questions.question: Two sources of 400 Hz and 403 Hz are sounded together. How many beats are heard in 5 seconds?
questions.explanation:
Beat frequency \( =403-400=3 \) per second.

In 5 s: \( 3\times5=15 \) beats.
questions.hint: Find beats per second first.
distractor_logic: Gives beats per second, not the number in 5 seconds
Trap D: uses the sum of frequencies
Trap D: uses the average frequency

questions.topic: Beats and the Doppler Effect
questions.question: A source of sound moves away from a stationary listener. Compared with the actual frequency, the frequency heard is:
options: Higher at first and then lower
questions.explanation:
A receding source stretches the waves behind it, making the wavelength longer.

Longer wavelength at the same wave speed means lower frequency: \( f'=f\,v/(v+v_s) \).
questions.hint: Moving away stretches the waves.
distractor_logic: Trap D: this is what happens when the source approaches
Ignores the Doppler effect
Mixes this with a source that first approaches and then passes the listener

questions.topic: Beats and the Doppler Effect
questions.question: When two sound waves of slightly different frequencies produce beats, the time between two successive loud sounds equals:
questions.explanation:
The loudness repeats at the beat frequency \( |f_1-f_2| \).

So the time between loud sounds is the beat period \( 1/|f_1-f_2| \).
questions.hint: Period is the reciprocal of frequency.
distractor_logic: Trap D: uses the sum of the frequencies
Gives the beat frequency, not the beat period
Trap D: uses the period of the average frequency

questions.topic: Transverse and Longitudinal Waves: the Wave Equation and Speed of a Wave
questions.question: A wave is given by \( y=0.05\sin(2x-10t) \) in SI units. What are its speed and direction of travel?
questions.explanation:
Compare with \( y=A\sin(kx-\omega t) \): here \( k=2 \) rad/m and \( \omega=10 \) rad/s.

Speed \( v=\omega/k=10/2=5 \) m/s.

The form \( kx-\omega t \) means travel along +x.
questions.hint: Read off k and \( \omega \), then use \( v=\omega/k \).
distractor_logic: Trap A: gets the speed right but links the minus sign with negative-direction travel
Trap A variant: uses \( v=\omega k \) instead of \( v=\omega/k \)
Uses \( k/\omega \), inverting the speed formula

questions.topic: Transverse and Longitudinal Waves: the Wave Equation and Speed of a Wave
questions.question: For the wave \( y=0.02\sin(\pi x+4\pi t) \) (SI units), what are the wavelength and the frequency?
questions.explanation:
Here \( k=\pi \) rad/m and \( \omega=4\pi \) rad/s.

\( \lambda=2\pi/k=2\pi/\pi=2 \) m.

\( f=\omega/2\pi=4\pi/2\pi=2 \) Hz. (The + sign only tells us the wave moves along -x; it does not change \( \lambda \) or \( f \).)
questions.hint: Use \( \lambda=2\pi/k \) and \( f=\omega/2\pi \).
distractor_logic: Inverts both relations, using \( \lambda=k/2\pi \) and \( f=2\pi/\omega \)
Reads k and \( \omega \) directly as wavelength and frequency
Divides \( \omega \) by \( \pi \) instead of \( 2\pi \) when finding frequency

questions.topic: Transverse and Longitudinal Waves: the Wave Equation and Speed of a Wave
questions.question: A string is stretched with a tension of 100 N and has a linear mass density of 0.01 kg/m. What is the speed of a transverse wave on it?
questions.hint: Tension over mass per unit length, then take the square root.
distractor_logic: Trap B: swaps the ratio and computes \( \sqrt{\mu/T} \)
Forgets the square root and uses \( T/\mu \)
Multiplies instead of dividing, computing \( \sqrt{T\mu} \)

questions.topic: Transverse and Longitudinal Waves: the Wave Equation and Speed of a Wave
questions.question: A 4 m long string has a total mass of 0.04 kg and is under a tension of 64 N. What is the speed of transverse waves on it?
questions.explanation:
Linear mass density \( \mu=0.04/4=0.01 \) kg/m.

\( v=\sqrt{64/0.01}=\sqrt{6400}=80 \) m/s.
questions.hint: First convert total mass into mass per metre.
distractor_logic: Trap B: uses total mass 0.04 kg in place of mass per unit length
Computes \( T/\mu \) and forgets the square root
Trap B: swaps tension and linear mass density

questions.topic: Transverse and Longitudinal Waves: the Wave Equation and Speed of a Wave
questions.question: For the wave \( y=0.01\sin(5x-200t) \) in SI units, what is the maximum speed of a particle of the medium?
questions.explanation:
Particle velocity is \( \partial y/\partial t=-A\omega\cos(kx-\omega t) \).

Its maximum magnitude is \( A\omega=0.01\times200=2 \) m/s.

This is different from the wave speed \( \omega/k=40 \) m/s.
questions.hint: Differentiate y with respect to time; the largest value of cosine is 1.
distractor_logic: Gives the wave speed \( \omega/k \), confusing the speed of the wave with the speed of a particle
Multiplies amplitude by k instead of by \( \omega \)
Takes \( \omega \) itself as a speed, ignoring the amplitude

questions.topic: Transverse and Longitudinal Waves: the Wave Equation and Speed of a Wave
questions.question: A vibrator sends waves along a stretched string. If the vibrator's frequency is doubled while the tension stays the same, what happens?
options: The wave speed doubles and the wavelength stays the same
The wave speed stays the same and the wavelength halves
The wave speed doubles and the wavelength also doubles
The wave speed halves and the wavelength stays the same
questions.explanation:
Speed on the string is \( v=\sqrt{T/\mu} \), fixed by the string and its tension.

With v fixed, \( v=f\lambda \) forces \( \lambda \) to halve when f doubles.
questions.hint: What decides wave speed on a string: the source or the string?
distractor_logic: Trap B: assumes wave speed depends on the wave's own frequency
Trap B, and it also breaks \( v=f\lambda \) since doubling f and \( \lambda \) would quadruple v
Trap B: makes speed depend on frequency, and in the wrong direction

questions.topic: Transverse and Longitudinal Waves: the Wave Equation and Speed of a Wave
questions.question: A wave of wavelength 2 m travels along a string. What is the phase difference between two points on the string 0.5 m apart along the direction of travel?
questions.explanation:
Phase difference \( \Delta\phi=k\Delta x=\dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}\Delta x \).

\( \Delta\phi=\dfrac{2\pi}{2}\times0.5=\dfrac{\pi}{2} \) rad.
questions.hint: One wavelength corresponds to \( 2\pi \) of phase.
distractor_logic: Treats 0.5 m as half a wavelength instead of a quarter
Uses \( \pi\Delta x/\lambda \), losing a factor of 2
Gives \( \Delta x/\lambda \) directly as an angle, leaving out \( 2\pi \)

questions.topic: Transverse and Longitudinal Waves: the Wave Equation and Speed of a Wave
questions.question: The tension in a stretched string is made four times its original value. The speed of transverse waves on it becomes:
options: Unchanged, since speed depends only on the wave's frequency
questions.explanation:
\( v=\sqrt{T/\mu} \), so \( v\propto\sqrt T \).

Making T four times gives \( \sqrt4=2 \) times the speed.
questions.hint: Speed goes as the square root of tension.
distractor_logic: Takes speed to be proportional to T rather than to \( \sqrt T \)
Inverts the dependence, as if speed fell with tension
Trap B: speed is set by the medium, and tension is part of that medium property

questions.topic: Speed of Sound and Waves in Different Media
questions.question: For a diatomic gas with \( \gamma=7/5 \), pressure \( 1.0\times10^5 \) Pa and density 0.875 kg per cubic metre, what is the speed of sound?
questions.explanation:
\( v=\sqrt{\gamma P/\rho} \).

\( \gamma P=1.4\times10^5 \) Pa, and \( 1.4\times10^5/0.875=1.6\times10^5 \).

\( v=\sqrt{1.6\times10^5}=400 \) m/s.
questions.hint: Use Laplace's formula, keeping the \( \gamma \).
distractor_logic: Trap B: Newton's uncorrected formula \( \sqrt{P/\rho} \), dropping \( \gamma \)
Uses \( \gamma^2P \) instead of \( \gamma P \)
Forgets to take the square root

questions.topic: Speed of Sound and Waves in Different Media
questions.question: The speed of sound in air at 300 K is 340 m/s. What is it at 1200 K?
questions.explanation:
\( v\propto\sqrt T \).

\( v_2=340\times\sqrt{1200/300}=340\times2=680 \) m/s.
questions.hint: Take the ratio of temperatures, then its square root.
distractor_logic: Takes speed proportional to T, not \( \sqrt T \)
Assumes the speed of sound in a given gas is fixed regardless of temperature
Uses the inverse square-root dependence

questions.topic: Speed of Sound and Waves in Different Media
questions.question: At the same temperature, what is the ratio of the speed of sound in hydrogen (molar mass 2 g/mol) to that in oxygen (molar mass 32 g/mol)? Both are diatomic.
questions.explanation:
\( v=\sqrt{\gamma RT/M} \); \( \gamma \) and T are the same.

\( v_H/v_O=\sqrt{M_O/M_H}=\sqrt{32/2}=\sqrt{16}=4 \).
questions.hint: Same \( \gamma \), same T, so only molar mass matters.
distractor_logic: Inverts the ratio; lighter gases carry sound faster, not slower
Uses the ratio of molar masses without taking the square root
Assumes same temperature means same speed, ignoring molar mass

questions.topic: Speed of Sound and Waves in Different Media
questions.question: A 500 Hz sound passes from air (speed 340 m/s) into water (speed 1500 m/s). What is its wavelength in water?
questions.explanation:
Frequency stays 500 Hz in water.

\( \lambda=v/f=1500/500=3 \) m.
questions.hint: Frequency carries over; speed changes.
distractor_logic: Keeps the wavelength from air, as if wavelength were fixed across media
Multiplies speed by frequency instead of dividing
Divides frequency by speed, inverting \( \lambda=v/f \)

questions.topic: Speed of Sound and Waves in Different Media
questions.question: Water has a bulk modulus of \( 2.25\times10^9 \) Pa and density 1000 kg per cubic metre. What is the speed of sound in water?
questions.explanation:
For a liquid, \( v=\sqrt{B/\rho} \).

\( B/\rho=2.25\times10^9/1000=2.25\times10^6 \).

\( v=\sqrt{2.25\times10^6}=1500 \) m/s.
questions.hint: Use bulk modulus over density, then take the root.
distractor_logic: Forgets the square root in \( \sqrt{B/\rho} \)
Takes the square root of the bulk modulus alone, ignoring density
Inverts the ratio to \( \sqrt{\rho/B} \)

questions.topic: Speed of Sound and Waves in Different Media
questions.question: At the same temperature and pressure, how does the speed of sound in moist air compare with that in dry air?
options: It is smaller in moist air
It is greater in moist air
It depends on the frequency of the sound
questions.explanation:
Water vapour (molar mass 18 g/mol) is lighter than dry air (about 29 g/mol).

So moist air has a lower density at the same pressure, and \( v=\sqrt{\gamma P/\rho} \) is larger.
questions.hint: Compare the molar mass of water with that of air.
distractor_logic: Assumes moist air is denser, but water vapour is lighter than the nitrogen and oxygen it replaces
Ignores the change in density caused by water vapour
Trap B: sound speed in a medium does not depend on frequency

questions.topic: Speed of Sound and Waves in Different Media
questions.question: For a monoatomic gas, by what factor does \( v^2 \) from Laplace's formula exceed \( v^2 \) from Newton's formula?
questions.explanation:
Laplace: \( v^2=\gamma P/\rho \). Newton: \( v^2=P/\rho \).

Ratio \( =\gamma \), which is \( 5/3 \) for a monoatomic gas.
questions.hint: Divide the two expressions for \( v^2 \).
distractor_logic: Gives the ratio of speeds, but the question asks for the ratio of squared speeds
Uses \( \gamma \) for a diatomic gas
Inverts the ratio, which would make Laplace's value the smaller one

questions.topic: Speed of Sound and Waves in Different Media
questions.question: At what temperature will the speed of sound in air be double its value at \( 27^\circ\text{C} \)?
questions.explanation:
\( 27^\circ\text{C}=300 \) K, and \( v\propto\sqrt T \).

Doubling v needs T multiplied by 4: \( T=1200 \) K.

\( 1200-273=927^\circ\text{C} \).
questions.hint: Work in kelvin; speed goes as \( \sqrt T \).

Doubles the Kelvin temperature, taking \( v\propto T \)

questions.topic: Superposition, Reflection, and Standing Waves
questions.question: A standing wave is given by \( y=0.04\sin(5\pi x)\cos(100\pi t) \) in SI units. What is the distance between adjacent nodes?
questions.explanation:
\( k=5\pi \) rad/m, so \( \lambda=2\pi/k=0.4 \) m.

Adjacent nodes are \( \lambda/2=0.2 \) m apart.
questions.hint: Find \( \lambda \) from k, then halve it.
distractor_logic: Gives the wavelength instead of half of it
Gives the node-to-antinode distance

questions.topic: Superposition, Reflection, and Standing Waves
questions.question: A standing wave \( y=0.06\sin kx\cos\omega t \) (in m) is formed by two travelling waves. What are the amplitude and directions of these component waves?
options: 0.03 m each, travelling in the same direction
0.03 m each, travelling in opposite directions
0.06 m each, travelling in opposite directions
0.12 m each, travelling in opposite directions
questions.explanation:
\( A\sin(kx-\omega t)+A\sin(kx+\omega t)=2A\sin kx\cos\omega t \).

Here \( 2A=0.06 \) m, so \( A=0.03 \) m, and the two waves move in opposite directions.
questions.hint: Compare with \( 2A\sin kx\cos\omega t \).
distractor_logic: Waves in the same direction combine into another travelling wave, not a standing wave
Forgets that the standing-wave amplitude is twice the component amplitude
Doubles instead of halving

questions.topic: Superposition, Reflection, and Standing Waves
questions.question: Two coherent sources emit waves of wavelength 0.4 m in phase. At a point P the path difference is 0.6 m. What happens at P?
options: Partially constructive, with amplitude 1.5 times that of one wave
It cannot be decided without the frequency
questions.explanation:
Path difference in wavelengths: \( 0.6/0.4=1.5 \), i.e. \( (1+\tfrac12)\lambda \).

This matches the destructive condition \( (n+\tfrac12)\lambda \).
questions.hint: Divide the path difference by the wavelength.
distractor_logic: Treats 0.6 m as a whole number of wavelengths, but it is 1.5 wavelengths
Misreads the number of wavelengths as an amplitude factor
Only the path difference compared with \( \lambda \) is needed

questions.topic: Superposition, Reflection, and Standing Waves
questions.question: Two pulses on a string, one upward of height 3 cm and one downward of depth 3 cm with the same shape, approach and pass through each other. Which is correct?
options: The pulses destroy each other permanently
At full overlap the displacement is 6 cm
The pulses bounce off each other and reverse direction
At full overlap the string is momentarily flat there, and afterwards both pulses continue unchanged
questions.explanation:
At full overlap: \( y=(+3)+(-3)=0 \), so the string is flat for an instant.

The energy is not lost; it is stored as kinetic energy of the string at that moment.

After passing, each pulse continues exactly as before.
questions.hint: Superposition affects only the overlap region, and only while they overlap.
distractor_logic: Superposition is temporary; each pulse continues with its own shape
Adds magnitudes, ignoring that the displacements have opposite signs
Waves pass through each other; they do not collide like particles

questions.topic: Superposition, Reflection, and Standing Waves
questions.question: Two waves \( y_1=A\sin(kx-\omega t) \) and \( y_2=A\sin(kx+\omega t) \) superpose. The result is:
options: A standing wave \( y=2A\sin kx\cos\omega t \)
A standing wave \( y=2A\cos kx\sin\omega t \)
A wave of amplitude \( 2A \) travelling along +x
questions.explanation:
Use \( \sin(a-b)+\sin(a+b)=2\sin a\cos b \) with \( a=kx \), \( b=\omega t \).

\( y=2A\sin kx\cos\omega t \): a standing wave, with positions fixed by \( \sin kx \) and time dependence by \( \cos\omega t \).
questions.hint: Apply the sin(a-b)+sin(a+b) identity.
distractor_logic: Swaps sine and cosine when applying the sum formula
Assumes the opposite signs of \( \omega t \) make the waves cancel completely
Two waves in opposite directions cannot give a net travelling wave

questions.question: For the standing wave \( y=2A\sin kx\cos\omega t \), where are the nodes located? (n = 0, 1, 2, ...)
questions.explanation:
Nodes need \( \sin kx=0 \), so \( kx=n\pi \).

With \( k=2\pi/\lambda \): \( x=n\lambda/2 \).
questions.hint: Set \( \sin kx=0 \).
distractor_logic: These are the antinode positions

questions.topic: Superposition, Reflection, and Standing Waves
questions.question: Two waves of equal amplitude A and equal frequency travel in the same direction with a phase difference of \( 2\pi/3 \). What is the amplitude of the resultant wave?
questions.explanation:
Resultant amplitude \( =2A\cos(\phi/2) \).

\( =2A\cos(\pi/3)=2A\times\tfrac12=A \).

questions.topic: Superposition, Reflection, and Standing Waves
questions.question: In a standing wave on a string, how do particles between two adjacent nodes vibrate relative to each other?
options: With phase changing steadily from point to point, as in a travelling wave
Each in opposite phase to its immediate neighbour
All with the same amplitude but random phases
All in the same phase, with different amplitudes
questions.explanation:
In \( y=2A\sin kx\cos\omega t \) every point shares the same \( \cos\omega t \).

Between two nodes \( \sin kx \) keeps one sign, so all these particles move together, in phase.

Across a node \( \sin kx \) changes sign, so neighbouring loops are in opposite phase.
questions.hint: Look at the time factor and the sign of \( \sin kx \) within one loop.
distractor_logic: This describes a travelling wave, not a standing wave
Opposite phase occurs only across a node, not between neighbours in the same loop
Amplitude varies with position and phases are not random

questions.topic: Normal Modes of Stretched Strings and Organ Pipes
questions.question: A pipe 0.85 m long is closed at one end. Taking the speed of sound as 340 m/s, what are its two lowest resonant frequencies?

questions.question: The fundamental of a pipe closed at one end is 150 Hz. Which of the following can also be a resonant frequency of this pipe?

questions.question: A string fixed at both ends vibrates in its fourth harmonic. How many nodes are there, including the two ends?
